title: NDIS participant homes and support-worker boundaries
audience: Cleaners and support workers who clean or assist in the homes of NDIS participants in any Australian state or territory. This is a new lesson with no source draft.
referencesAtStart: Official sources for this lesson: NDIS Practice Standards and Quality Indicators, Version 4 (November 2021), Core Module (no page date shown); NDIS worker screening (no date shown). Only part of the Practice Standards has been confirmed.
learningOutcomes: Explain that a participant's home is the participant's own home, and that the participant's choices, privacy and consent govern the work.
Describe how the NDIS Practice Standards treat environmental cleaning in participants' homes compared with other settings.
Identify the boundaries of a cleaner's or support worker's role in a participant's home, including household items, personal care and clinical tasks.
State the stop-and-refer steps when a request or a hazard is outside the agreed scope.

instruction.heading: Whose home it is
instruction.body: When you work in an NDIS participant's home, you are a guest in someone's home. The participant decides how the home is used, who may enter, what may be moved, and what they want done. Your agreed task is the scope, and the participant's wishes within that scope come first. Respect the participant's privacy, their belongings and their routines. Knock or announce yourself, ask before entering rooms the participant is not in, and do not read papers, open drawers or look through personal items. The participant may have other people living in the home, and their privacy matters too.

instruction.heading: How the standards treat cleaning in homes
instruction.body: The NDIS Practice Standards and Quality Indicators, Version 4 of November 2021, Core Module, require that infection prevention and control standard precautions are implemented in every setting where supports are provided. The routine environmental cleaning indicator applies in settings other than participants' homes, and it expressly excludes participants' homes. This is not a reason for a worker to ignore hygiene in a home. Standard precautions, hand hygiene, PPE use and safe handling of waste still apply to the worker's own conduct, and the participant's agreed support plan defines what cleaning, if any, is part of the service.

instruction.heading: Boundaries of the role in a home
instruction.body: Your role in a participant's home is the agreed support, and nothing more. Cleaning of the participant's own home is done only if it is part of the agreed service and the support plan. Do not perform clinical tasks, administer medication, change or manage equipment the participant uses for health reasons, or make decisions about care. Do not move or use the participant's assistive equipment beyond what the plan allows. Do not discard or sort the participant's belongings, medicines or waste unless the plan and the participant ask you to do so, and then only as directed. If a task is outside the plan, tell the participant and the provider, and do not do it.

instruction.heading: Hazards in a participant's home
instruction.body: Homes are not set up as clinical settings. A home may have soiled items, pets, unsafe steps, mould, chemicals stored in unsafe places, or needles or medical waste from the participant's own care. Stop and assess before you start if a hazard is present, and do not handle sharps, body fluid or unknown waste by hand. Report the hazard to the provider and, where a participant is at risk, to the appropriate contact. Where the home has a hazard that the provider's risk assessment does not cover, the work pauses until the provider decides how it is managed. Mould and other serious hazards in homes can be outside your role and need specialist assessment.

instruction.heading: Worked scenario: the participant asks for something else
instruction.body: A participant asks you, while you are there to clean the kitchen, to help them take their medication and to sort through a box of old papers. Neither task is in your agreed support plan. Medication administration and clinical tasks are outside your role, and sorting papers is outside the scope unless the plan includes it. Politely explain that you can only do the agreed tasks, record the request, and tell your supervisor and the provider the same day so the plan can be reviewed. Do not do the tasks, and do not refuse in a way that leaves the participant without a safe alternative. The provider should arrange it.

procedure: Read the support plan and confirm the agreed tasks for the visit before you start.
Announce yourself, ask the participant where to work, and confirm which rooms and items are in scope.
Check the area for hazards, including sharps, body fluid, unknown waste and unsafe conditions, before starting.
Carry out only the agreed tasks, with the participant's consent and within their wishes.
If the participant asks for a task outside the plan, decline politely, record the request, and tell the provider the same day.
If a hazard is found that the provider's assessment does not cover, stop that part of the work and notify the provider.
Record the tasks completed, the requests declined, any hazard, and the person notified, with the time.

workedExamples.situation: You are booked to clean a participant's bathroom. The participant asks you to also empty a bin of used needles from their own care, saying they keep it in the cupboard.
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not handle the needles or the bin. Sharps and medical waste from the participant's own care are not in the cleaning scope, and they are not to be handled by hand. Explain politely that you cannot do that, record the request, and tell the provider and the participant's nominated contact the same day so that a safe disposal can be arranged under the plan. Continue with the bathroom only if the area is safe.

workedExamples.situation: A participant's home has a strong smell and visible dark staining on a wall near the bathroom. The support plan asks for a general clean of the house.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Do you start the general clean?
workedExamples.reasoning: Pause before starting. Visible staining and a smell may indicate a hazard, such as mould, that is outside the general clean and needs specialist assessment. Do not start the general clean in the affected area. Tell the provider, record what you saw and the time, and wait for the provider to decide how it is managed.

commonErrors.error: Doing a task that is not in the support plan because the participant asked for it.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the plan. Decline politely, record the request, and tell the provider the same day.

commonErrors.error: Assuming that because a home is not a clinical setting, hygiene and PPE do not apply.
commonErrors.prevention: Standard precautions, hand hygiene and safe handling of waste apply to your own conduct in every home.

commonErrors.error: Handling needles or medical waste from a participant's own care by hand.
commonErrors.prevention: Do not handle sharps or medical waste by hand. Report them and arrange safe disposal through the provider.

commonErrors.error: Starting a general clean in an area with a suspected hazard such as mould.
commonErrors.prevention: Pause the affected area, report, and wait for the provider's assessment.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: The NDIS Practice Standards and Quality Indicators, Version 4 of November 2021, Core Module, require that infection prevention and control standard precautions are implemented throughout all settings where supports are provided. Routine environmental cleaning is required in settings other than participants' homes.

Licence notice: A worker delivering NDIS supports and services may need an NDIS worker screening clearance, and a condition of provider registration is to fulfil worker screening requirements. This lesson does not grant a screening clearance or any registration. Confirm the requirement for each role with the provider.

Handling sharps, medical waste and body fluid in a participant's home is outside a cleaner's or support worker's role under this lesson. Where such items are present, the provider arranges safe handling and disposal.
Mould and other serious hazards in homes require specialist assessment. This course does not teach mould remediation, and any such work is outside the cleaner's role.

qualityStandard: The learner identifies, in three supplied requests, which are within the support plan, which are declined, and what is recorded for each.
The learner pauses work and notifies the provider for two supplied hazards, without handling the hazard.
The learner states, without prompting, that the participant's home is the participant's, and describes the privacy steps for entering rooms.
The learner records the tasks completed, the requests declined and the person notified, with the time.
documentationEvidence: Tasks completed against the support plan, and any restriction applied
Requests declined, with the request, the person who made it, and the provider notified
Hazards found, the action taken, the person notified and the time
summary: A participant's home is the participant's. Their wishes and privacy govern the work, within the agreed plan.
Clinical tasks, medication, and out-of-plan tasks are outside your role. Decline, record and notify the provider.
Standard precautions, hand hygiene and safe handling of waste apply to your own conduct in every home.
Pause on any hazard the provider has not assessed, including sharps, medical waste and suspected mould.

knowledgeChecks.question: A participant asks you to help them take their medication during a cleaning visit. What is the correct response?
options: Decline politely, because medication administration is outside your role, record the request, and tell the provider the same day.
Help them, since they asked and it is a small task that takes only a minute of your time to do properly.
Hold the medication while they take it, without giving advice, since that is only a small part of the visit.

knowledgeChecks.question: How do the NDIS Practice Standards treat routine environmental cleaning in participants' homes?
options: The standards require routine environmental cleaning in every participant's home, in the same way as a clinic.
The standards require routine environmental cleaning in settings other than participants' homes.
The standards prohibit all cleaning in participants' homes.

knowledgeChecks.question: You find a used needle in a bin in a participant's bathroom. What is the correct action?
options: Remove it with a tissue and place it in the household bin, since the tissue protects the hand.
Leave it, because it is outside the cleaning task and nobody will touch it while you work.
Do not handle it by hand. Report it to the provider and arrange safe disposal through the plan.
